objectives: Avoid reflex antimalarial retreatment when malaria testing is negative.
Use focused history and exam to broaden differential diagnosis in persistent fever.
Choose targeted management and clear safety-net advice based on available findings.
takeaways: A negative RDT in a stable teen should trigger broader assessment, not repeat AL.
Recent incomplete response to antimalarials is a clue to reconsider the working diagnosis.
Match treatment to evidence and document return precautions clearly.
learnCaseOverrides.blurb: A teenager has persistent fever despite prior antimalarials and a negative RDT today. Decide how to avoid anchoring and treat what the chart supports.

sections.title: Chief complaint
sections.text: Fever for 5 days despite antimalarials from a drug shop

sections.title: Triage note
sections.text: Family requests 'strong malaria medicine again' because fever returned.

coach.title: Mercy has persistent fever
coach.body: She is alert, drinking, and speaking normally, but still febrile after treatment she received elsewhere.
coach.quote: “She took malaria tablets already, but fever is still there.”

teach.label: Clinical framing
teach.text: When the current malaria test is negative, avoid anchoring and actively search for another source of fever.

coach.title: How do you respond to this result?
coach.body: She is stable but still febrile. Pick the action that avoids common overtreatment errors.

question.prompt: What is the best next step now?

options.text: Broaden the workup for other causes of fever and do a focused re-exam
Repeat artemether-lumefantrine immediately because she still has fever
Give injectable antimalarial to be extra safe
Discharge without further assessment because malaria is ruled out

question.right: Correct. With RDT negative and no danger signs on this chart, Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 support investigating non-malarial fever causes rather than automatic antimalarial retreatment.
question.wrong: This chart already shows a negative RDT today. Repeating antimalarials without new evidence risks missing the real cause of Mercy's fever.

sections.title: Focused history reveal
sections.text: No convulsions, no confusion, no neck stiffness. Dysuria and suprapubic discomfort started 2 days ago.

coach.title: Which action best fits these findings?
coach.body: You now have urinary symptoms and supportive urine results.

options.text: Treat likely urinary tract infection per local guideline and provide fever follow-up advice
Ignore urine findings and give another malaria course anyway
Start dual antimalarial and antibiotic treatment without documenting rationale
Withhold all treatment and ask family to buy medicines privately

question.right: Correct. Dysuria plus nitrite-positive urine supports a non-malarial source of fever; targeted treatment and review planning are safer than reflex malaria retreatment.
question.wrong: These findings point away from malaria and toward urinary infection. Ignoring them repeats the same anchoring error that delayed improvement.

sections.title: Plan
sections.detail: Likely UTI treatment + antipyretic + hydration advice

sections.title: Safety-net before discharge
sections.reveal_note: Caregiver understands when to return urgently.

coach.title: What discharge counseling is essential?
coach.body: Even stable patients need explicit return precautions.

options.text: Explain likely non-malarial cause, review danger signs, and schedule prompt follow-up if not improving
Tell family any recurrent fever is definitely malaria next time
Provide treatment but no warning signs to avoid alarming them
Advise stopping treatment once fever falls on day 1

question.right: Correct. Mercy is stable now, but persistent fever needs clear safety-netting and planned reassessment if she does not improve.
question.wrong: Without explicit return guidance, persistent or worsening fever can be missed. Counseling is part of safe febrile illness management.

sections.title: Case outcome
sections.text: You avoided repeat antimalarial treatment after a negative RDT and managed based on new evidence.
sections.emphasis: Persistent fever requires structured reassessment, not automatic retreatment.

coach.title: Key teaching points
coach.body: This case tests anchoring bias. Mercy's negative malaria test, stable vitals, and urinary findings justified broadening the differential and choosing targeted treatment. Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 support test-guided malaria care and clear follow-up safety-netting.

teach.label: Clinician review
teach.text: In persistent fever, the best next step is often a better question and focused exam, not another empiric malaria course.
